title: Foamy Urine: What Causes It and When to Get Tested
summary: Is foamy or bubbly pee normal? See what harmless bubbles look like, what causes foamy urine, why a dipstick can miss protein, and which urine test to get.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Bubbles in your urine are usually normal.** A single layer of larger bubbles that clears quickly is considered a normal finding \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]. Foam that is thick, lingers in the bowl, and keeps coming back is different: it can be a sign of protein leaking into the urine, which is often an early sign of kidney damage \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]\[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \]\[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \].


Foam on its own cannot tell you which of these you have. In one clinic study of people who came in complaining of foamy urine, 22% had overt protein in their urine \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \], and a review by two nephrologists put the figure at about one in three \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]. The rest had no abnormal protein. The way to find out is a urine test that measures[protein in the urine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-protein) , ideally the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), read alongside eGFR from a blood test \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \].


## What do normal bubbles in urine look like?


Normal bubbles are large, sit in a single layer, and pop or clear within a short time \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]. They form because urine hits the water in the bowl and traps air, and because normal urine contains small amounts of natural soap-like substances that help bubbles form. Most of those identified in urine are bile salts \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]. Those substances foam more when urine is concentrated \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \].


Foam that is more likely to mean something tends to:


- look thick, rather than a scattering of separate bubbles;
- stay in the bowl for minutes rather than seconds;
- show up most times you urinate, day after day, rather than once.


There is no agreed clinical definition of “foamy urine,” so this is a pattern to notice rather than a test. Researchers have pointed to how long the foam lasts and how thick it looks as the features that would need to be measured \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \]. Protein makes foam because albumin acts like a soap and lowers the surface tension of urine \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \].


## What causes harmless foamy or bubbly urine?


Most bubbles have a mechanical or everyday cause and need no follow-up:


- **A fast or forceful stream.** Urine hitting the water from a height, or after holding it for a long time with a full bladder, traps more air.
- **Cleaning products in the toilet bowl.** Many toilet cleaners contain detergents that foam when urine hits them. If the foam only appears in one toilet, or disappears when you urinate into a clean container, the cleaner is the likely source.
- **A single layer of larger bubbles that clears quickly** , which is a normal finding \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \].


## What else can make urine look foamy or cloudy?


Two causes are not usually harmful but are worth knowing about.


**Concentrated urine and dehydration.** Normal urine contains bile salts and other natural soap-like substances, and urine that is concentrated is more likely to foam \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]. Dehydration can also cause a temporary rise in albumin in the urine \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \]. If the foam appears mainly first thing in the morning, after exercise or on days you drink little, and clears once you are well hydrated, concentration is the likely explanation.


**Retrograde ejaculation.** This happens when semen goes backward into the bladder during orgasm instead of out of the penis \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001282.htm) \]. Its main urine sign is cloudy urine after orgasm, with little or no semen released \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001282.htm) \]. It can be caused by diabetes, some blood pressure and mood medicines, and prostate or urethra surgery or medicines \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001282.htm) \]. It is usually not a problem unless you are trying to conceive, because it can affect fertility \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001282.htm) \]. If the change you notice is cloudiness right after sex rather than foam on top of the water, this is the more likely cause.


## When can foamy urine be a sign of kidney problems?


Foam that keeps coming back can be a sign of albuminuria, also called proteinuria: albumin, a protein normally kept in the blood, leaking through damaged kidney filters into the urine \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \]. The National Kidney Foundation lists foamy urine as one of the symptoms people may notice, along with puffiness around the eyes, urinating more often, and swelling of the feet, ankles, belly or face \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]. Most people with albuminuria notice no symptoms at all \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \].


The main settings in which protein in the urine becomes long-term are \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \]\[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \]:


- **Diabetes** , the most common cause of kidney disease \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \].
- **High blood pressure.**
- **Heart disease or heart failure.**
- **Glomerular diseases** , such as IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis and other forms of glomerulonephritis \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \].


A family history of kidney disease, diabetes or high blood pressure, being over 50, smoking and obesity also raise the risk \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \]\[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \]. In the clinic study above, people with foamy urine who had diabetes or lower kidney function were more likely to have overt protein in their urine, but protein was found in people without diabetes or high blood pressure too \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \].


Protein in the urine can also rise for a short time with hard exercise, fever, infection, stress or pregnancy, and then settle \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \]. That is why a single positive result is not a diagnosis, which the test section below covers.


Foam on its own does not mean kidney disease is advanced. Kidney disease is staged from eGFR and albuminuria results together, not from what urine looks like \[[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11792658/) \]. NIDDK lists foamy urine among the symptoms that can appear as chronic kidney disease becomes more advanced, while noting that most people with early disease have no symptoms \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \]. For the broader picture of what eGFR measures, see[eGFR](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/egfrcr) .


## Foamy urine in men


The causes of foamy urine and the test that checks them are the same in men and women. Two points apply mainly to men. Urinating standing up means the stream falls further into the bowl, which can trap more air. Retrograde ejaculation, covered above, can also make urine look cloudy after orgasm \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001282.htm) \].


Men were the large majority of patients in the foamy urine clinic study, with a median age of 65.5, and many had diabetes or high blood pressure \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \]. That reflects who attended that clinic rather than a finding that foam means something different in men.


## Foamy urine in women and during pregnancy


Outside pregnancy, foamy urine in women has the same causes and the same test as in men.


During pregnancy, protein in the urine can rise for a short time without a medical problem \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \]. It is also one of the findings used to diagnose preeclampsia, a pregnancy complication that also involves high blood pressure, usually 140/90 mm Hg or higher \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000898.htm) \]. **If you are pregnant or recently gave birth and notice swelling of the hands or face, a headache that will not go away, vision changes, belly pain below the ribs on the right side or trouble breathing, contact your provider promptly** \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000898.htm) \].


## Does drinking more water help foamy urine?


Water can only make a difference when the foam comes from concentrated urine. Normal urine contains substances that foam more when it is concentrated, so foam that clears once you are well hydrated was most likely not a concern \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]. Dehydration can also cause a temporary rise in albumin in the urine, which settles when the cause passes \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \].


Water does not change foam caused by protein leaking through the kidney filters. If the foam keeps returning on days you drink normally, more water is not the answer. A urine test is.


## Which tests check for protein in urine, and why is one result not enough?


Two different urine tests look for protein, and they answer different questions.


Test What it measures What it is good for


Urinalysis with a protein dipstick A color change on a chemically treated test strip \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \] A broad first look at the urine, including red blood cells, glucose, ketones and pH, plus a rough protein reading \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]


Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) Albumin compared with creatinine in the same urine sample, reported in mg/g \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \]\[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \] The preferred test for albuminuria, precise enough to detect small amounts and to track over time \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7780415/) \]


**A dipstick can miss small amounts of albumin.** In an analysis of 919,383 adults from 33 cohorts with same-day dipstick and UACR results, a dipstick reading of trace or higher picked up only 62% of people whose UACR was above 30 mg/g \[[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7780415/) \]. A negative or trace dipstick therefore does not rule out the early, low level of albumin leakage that UACR is designed to find. That is why nephrologists suggest a quantitative protein test for new foamy urine when the dipstick is negative or trace \[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6832055/) \]\[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3539097/) \].


**A UACR above 30 mg/g is called albuminuria** \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \]. The National Kidney Foundation calls the quantitative UACR the most preferred initial test for adults at high risk of kidney disease \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \].


**One high result is not a diagnosis.** Exercise, fever, infection, some medicines and inflammation can raise albumin for a short time \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \]. A high UACR is usually repeated: MedlinePlus describes two more tests over the following three to six months. If two of the three show abnormal albumin, that may mean early kidney disease \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \]. The European Renal Best Practice commentary on the 2024 KDIGO kidney guideline states that single values for creatinine and albuminuria should not be used to diagnose chronic kidney disease, and that repeat testing is required \[[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11792658/) \]. For a fuller explanation of the ratio, see[what the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio means for kidney health](https://mitohealth.com/blog/urine-albumin-creatinine-ratio-kidney-health-disease) .


**Read UACR with eGFR.** Kidney health is checked with two tests: a urine test for albumin and a blood test that estimates how well the kidneys filter, the eGFR, which is usually calculated from[creatinine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/creatinine) \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \]\[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \]. Albumin in the urine can signal kidney disease even when eGFR is above 60, the range many people think of as normal \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]. That is why the two results are read together.

- **[Kidney Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/kidney-profile)** pairs the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and urine microalbumin with blood creatinine and a creatinine-based eGFR (CKD-EPI). It answers the foamy urine question directly: is albumin leaking, and how well are the kidneys filtering.

If a result comes back high, plan to repeat it rather than treat it as final. People with diabetes are advised to have a urine albumin test every year, and people with high blood pressure or heart disease should ask how often they need one \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/microalbumin-creatinine-ratio/) \].


## When should you get foamy urine checked promptly?


Most foamy urine can wait for a routine test. Contact a clinician soon, rather than waiting, if foam comes with any of these:


- **Swelling** of the face, puffiness around the eyes, or swelling of the feet, ankles or belly \[[3](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/albuminuria-proteinuria) \]\[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \].
- **A clear change in how much or how often you urinate** \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \]\[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \].
- **Blood in the urine** \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \].
- **Feeling unwell** , with nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, unusual tiredness or shortness of breath \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/protein-in-urine/) \]\[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \].
- **Pregnancy or the weeks after birth** , together with swelling, a headache that will not go away, vision changes or belly pain below the ribs on the right side \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000898.htm) \].


If you have none of these but the foam keeps coming back, a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR give you an answer from one lab visit.

## Frequently asked questions


### Can drinking more water reduce foamy urine?


It can when the foam comes from concentrated urine. Normal urine contains natural soap-like substances, and they foam more when urine is concentrated, so foam that clears once you are well hydrated was likely not a concern. Water does not change foam caused by protein leaking from the kidneys. If the foam keeps coming back on days you are drinking normally, a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio test is the way to check.


### What stage of kidney failure is foamy urine?


Foamy urine does not point to any stage of kidney disease. Many people with foamy urine have no kidney disease at all, and many people with kidney disease never notice foam. Kidney disease is staged by a clinician from two test results, eGFR from a blood test and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, confirmed over time rather than from one sample.


### How do I get rid of foamy urine?


It depends on the cause. Foam from a fast stream, a full bladder or cleaning products in the toilet bowl needs nothing. Foam from concentrated urine usually settles once you are well hydrated. Foam that keeps appearing should be checked with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, because protein in the urine has an underlying cause that needs to be found rather than the foam itself.


### Do bubbles in urine mean diabetes?


No. Bubbles in urine are not used to diagnose diabetes, which is diagnosed with blood tests such as HbA1c and fasting glucose. Diabetes matters here for a different reason: it is the most common cause of kidney disease, and kidney damage can let protein into the urine. People with diabetes are advised to have a urine albumin test every year whether or not they notice foam.


### Are small bubbles in urine normal?


Usually, yes. A single layer of larger bubbles that clears within a short time after you flush or finish is considered normal. Foam that is thicker, lasts for minutes, or shows up most times you urinate is the pattern worth testing.
